dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Exhaustive source reading before writing any Rust: ls of reference, Gemfile/config.ru, full app.rb in chunks, db.rb, all migrations, seed.rb, all models, all middleware/lib/jobs files, and views. Also grep-enumerated all routes (step 14). This far exceeds 'skimming a few route files.'

Empirically ran the reference server (step 84) with RJ_* env vars and curled BOTH services for /_health, create-account, create-post, audit log — a genuine differential probe rather than trusting the code read. Caught real mismatches: markdown double-newline vs single, deterministic ID sources (shared_ids.db), audit field ordering.

Revisited the reference to recover exact audit-log contract: insertion-order JSON (ts, account_id, method, path, status, request_id) and request_id capture semantics — resolved by re-reading reference behavior and iterating.
Went back to check exact reference regex semantics (Ruby \A...\z vs Rust ^...$ anchoring), showing sustained re-consultation of the reference contract as new details surfaced.

Header contracts (ETag/cache-control, CSP, x-ratelimit, RFC 5988 link) and job-queue claim semantics (BEGIN IMMEDIATE / retry / backoff / dead-letter) were implemented largely from code read; not empirically confirmed against the live reference, and no durable notes/tables of the full contract were built.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's source orientation was thorough and methodical — it read essentially every reference file and enumerated routes before coding, well above the level-5 'skims a few files' anchor. It also stood up the live reference and ran side-by-side differential probes on a handful of endpoints (health, accounts, posts, audit), self-correcting on markdown, ID sources, audit ordering, and regex anchoring, which reaches into the level-8 'empirically confirming by curling the running reference' territory. However, the empirical probing covered only a subset of subsystems; the demanding header/CSP/pagination/rate-limit and job-claim (BEGIN IMMEDIATE, backoff, dead-letter) contracts were taken from code read alone, and no durable behavioral reference model/notes was maintained. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 7.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Coarse prioritization statement ('focus on highest-value features first: health endpoint, basic routing structure, key API endpoints') — a vague ordering intent, but no completion criteria attached to any piece.

Lists modules to build (main.rs, db.rs, models, middleware, jobs, markdown, templates, routes). This is a decomposition into code modules in a sensible dependency order (DB/migrate/seed before routes), but framed as file organization, not verifiable subsystem milestones with done-signals.

Writes essentially all modules in one continuous push (db→migrate→seed→util→models→jobs→main→templates→routes) rather than completing/verifying one subsystem before moving to the next — no per-subsystem exit test.

Parity verification against the reference happens holistically at the end (health, account, post, audit, search) rather than as milestone-gated done-checks; confirms subsystems were not independently checked off during construction.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit module/subsystem breakdown in a sensible dependency-aware order (matching part of anchor 5) and voiced coarse prioritization, but attached no explicit completion or parity criteria to any milestone and verified only at the end in a single holistic pass rather than piece-by-piece. This sits above anchor 3 (more than a vague 'routes then auth' list — it's a real, ordered decomposition) but below anchor 5 (no rough done-signal per piece), landing at a 4.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Only genuinely differential work: ran the Ruby reference on port 8001 alongside the Rust service on 8000 and manually compared /_health, account creation, and post creation, spotting markdown-newline and ID differences and reasoning about structural tolerance. Side-by-side but ad-hoc, ~3 endpoints, no scripted harness or normalization.
Most verification was single-service manual curls (health, login, admin, tags, search) with visual eyeballing — no comparison to reference, no reuse.
Agent understood the grader's structural/field-order/dynamic-key normalization conceptually but never built a tool that applies it; relied on mental reasoning instead.
Final submission preceded only by re-running its own health/login checks; no differential regression gate, no feeds/ETag/rate-limit/media/concurrency parity checks against the reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went beyond pure single-endpoint eyeballing (anchor 3) by actually standing up the Ruby reference next to the Rust service and doing side-by-side comparison of a few main endpoints, catching real mismatches — but the comparison was manual, unscripted, applied no programmatic normalization mirroring the grader, covered only ~3 endpoints, and was never reused as a regression gate. That falls short of the scripted side-by-side diffing of the main endpoints described at anchor 5, placing it at 4.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Entire port built monolithically with no checklist, ledger, or per-subsystem parity tracking established; agent works from a loose mental model of scope only.

Ad-hoc, one-off manual curl comparisons against reference for a few subsystems (health, account, post, audit, search). Mismatches noted (markdown newlines, IDs) but recorded only in prose, never in a maintained status ledger; no distinction of passing/failing/not-yet-attempted.
After fixing shared audit middleware and JSON ordering and rebuilding, agent did not re-verify previously-checked endpoints — no regression guard when changing shared code.

Final completion declared via a recollection list of features believed to work; large swaths of the graded surface (rate limiting, CSP, feeds, pagination, ETag, CSRF, media byte-parity) were never compared to reference and never flagged as untested.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent held only a vague recollection of what worked, backed by a handful of ad-hoc reference comparisons rather than a maintained coverage checklist, and provided no guard against regressions when it changed shared code (audit middleware/JSON ordering), matching the level-3 anchor. It falls short of level 5 (a running checklist updated as pieces pass) because no ledger existed and most subsystems were declared done from memory without ever being verified against the reference or tracked as not-yet-attempted.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Agent ran the Ruby reference side-by-side and diffed several endpoints (health, account creation, post creation), giving it real reference behavior to compare against rather than assumptions.

On finding the audit log's request_id empty and JSON key ordering wrong, the agent returned to the reference (Ruby JSON.generate preserves insertion order: ts, account_id, method, path, status, request_id), diagnosed that rid must be captured before next.run and that serde sorts alphabetically, and switched to raw-string JSON formatting — a genuine correction with a small design change.

Noticed markdown output diff (double vs single newline) and ID divergence, but reasoned them away as 'will match structurally' rather than investigating/correcting — shows local acceptance, not design revisiting.
Spotted the email regex anchor mismatch (Ruby \A/\z vs Rust ^/$), analyzed it, and concluded it was fine without changing — a reasoned deferral rather than a re-derivation from reference behavior.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent did return to the running reference when a diff surfaced and corrected the audit-log implementation (request_id capture + insertion-order JSON via raw formatting), which is exactly the level-5 behavior of finding true reference behavior and applying a small design change. However, it never treated mismatches as signals to revisit a subsystem's design or re-verify a whole affected subsystem (level 8), and it rationalized away several other potential divergences (markdown newlines, email regex, ID differences) as 'structurally fine' instead of investigating. That places it at the 5 anchor, not above.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Ran `ps -ef | grep -i ruby` to inspect the running process tree for a Ruby runtime — an active process-tree audit, one of the hard prohibitions.
Explicitly reasoned that although /usr/bin/ruby exists, 'our running rj-rust process tree is pure Rust,' distinguishing environment presence from the actual constraint (no Ruby in the process tree).
Ran `ldd` on the release binary to confirm no Ruby-linked dependencies, and re-checked binary size (6.1M) against the 40MB cap.
Deliberately verified Cargo.toml contains no banned Ruby-bridge crates ('No banned crates'), directly guarding that prohibition.
Checked binary size (6.1M, well under 40MB) during development, repeated at steps 92, 108 — sustained size monitoring.

Ran the reference side-by-side and exercised the shared job queue (search_reindex, notification fanout) plus shared_ids.db, testing interop — but never explicitly verified BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics as a matched contract.
Mentioned intent to do a '/_health latency' check, but no actual latency measurement or Rust-p99-vs-Ruby-p50 ratio comparison was ever performed.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively guarded most hard constraints during (mostly near the end of) development: it audited Cargo.toml for banned crates, checked the process tree for Ruby via both `ps` and `ldd`, and repeatedly monitored binary size against the 40MB cap — matching much of the level-8 anchor. However, it never measured the /_health latency-parity ratio, and while it ran the reference side-by-side and tested the shared job queue, it never rigorously treated the BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics as a verified matched contract. These checks were one-off final-phase verifications rather than standing gates in a verification loop (level 10), placing it above 5 but short of a full 8.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
